claims.text: The starting material is a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix produced by powder metallurgy without a self-lubricating phase.
The intervention is the addition of 3–5 vol.% h-BN nanoplatelets to the CoCrFeNi matrix.
Powder metallurgy followed by hot pressing will produce uniform dispersion of the h-BN nanoplatelets.
The dispersed h-BN nanoplatelets will remain thermally stable from room temperature to 800 °C during sliding in ambient air.
The h-BN nanoplatelets will align during sliding.
Aligned h-BN nanoplatelets will form a continuous lubricious tribofilm on the wear surface.
h-BN has intrinsically low shear strength along its basal planes.
The h-BN tribofilm will adapt to changes associated with thermal expansion and oxidation over the tested temperature range.
The continuous h-BN tribofilm will reduce interfacial shear and thereby lower friction.
The continuous h-BN tribofilm will protect the wear surface and thereby reduce wear.
Relative to unmodified CoCrFeNi, the h-BN-modified alloy will exhibit a lower and more stable coefficient of friction from room temperature to 800 °C.
Relative to unmodified CoCrFeNi, the h-BN-modified alloy will exhibit a lower wear rate from room temperature to 800 °C.
The predicted effectiveness is limited to sliding in ambient air and to the variable-load range used in the proposed tests.
Non-uniform nanoplatelet dispersion may cause aggregation and reduce effectiveness.
Severe oxidation under high load may compromise tribofilm integrity.
Dispersion and interfacial bonding may impede consistent tribofilm formation, especially under high-load oxidizing conditions.
Failure to obtain statistically significant friction reduction and stabilization together with lower wear across the tested temperatures would falsify the hypothesis.
